retail_intro: The weekend handed the crowd two kinds of conviction, Buffett's patience in a letter that laments a lack of good investments [[n0807]] and the war trade's new sovereign buyer in Germany, and both rest on the same old mechanism: buy what you trust most when everyone else is frightened.

retail.title: Berkshire Hathaway Class B / BRK-B — Buffett's letter lands in a war market
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Once a year the crowd gets one shareholder letter it actually reads, and this year it landed in the middle of a war. The story retail tells itself about Berkshire is the opposite of a meme: the oldest hand in the market stays calm, buys back his own stock and lets the noise pass. Buffett repurchased a record $27 billion of Berkshire stock in 2021 as operating earnings surged [[n0806]]. The shares had closed Friday, before the letter, at $319.24, up 3.56% on the day and 1.81% over five sessions in which the S&P 500 managed 0.10% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25), so Monday is the first session to price it. The emotional hook is safety by proxy: if you cannot stomach the war tape yourself, own the investor who can.
What Is Driving It

The letter is the catalyst, and its headlines are built for retail. Buffett called Apple one of the Four Giants driving Berkshire's value [[n0828]], and Forbes Middle East puts Berkshire's 2021 net profit at $89.8B [[n0837]], numbers that read like a fortress. The letter came out on Saturday, after an invasion week that ended with the S&P 500 up 2.24% on Friday at 4,384.65 index points and the VIX down 2.73 points to 27.59, while Apple rose 1.30% to $164.85 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25). Then the weekend escalated: the US and Europe moved to bar some Russian banks from SWIFT [[n1412]] and Germany committed €100 billion to defence [[n1228]].
The Social Signal

The attention is broad for a shareholder letter, and it is the copy-the-master kind. MoneyWise was already walking readers through four of Buffett's most notable fourth-quarter portfolio changes [[n0738]], Yahoo Finance is running a piece on Buffett's fourth law of motion [[n0876]], and Time led with the mildly attractive path of $27 billion in buybacks [[n0827]]. The same weekend, CNBC asked readers whether they panic sold during the week's volatility and when to get back into the market [[n1969]]. The pattern implies a crowd looking for permission to stay invested, and Berkshire's letter is the most trusted permission slip on offer.
Historical Analog

The analog the Buffett crowd reaches for is Buffett himself. CNBC's read before the letter was that for Berkshire the big issues haven't changed [[n0731]], and Business Insider's reminder that Buffett avoids Russia over threats of violence and asset seizure [[n0393]] looks, after a week of sanctions, like the old discipline paying off in plain sight. The mechanism is the anti-meme. Berkshire compounds through cash-generating businesses and buys itself back when nothing better is on offer, so it is built to look dull in manias and sturdy in drawdowns. Over 20 sessions the stock is up 3.76% against 1.34% for the S&P 500 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25), a margin made of patience rather than leverage.
Smart Money View

Here the smart money is the letter, and it is less bullish than the crowd's reading. Reuters says Buffett lamented a lack of good investments even as Berkshire's profit set a record [[n0807]]; a manager who laments a shortage of good investments is not calling a bottom. The bull reading has support too, since CNBC frames Apple as one of the Four Giants driving Berkshire's value [[n0828]], and Business Insider's account of Buffett blasting fake earnings [[n0826]] can be read as a jab at the profitless growth stories retail chased in 2021. And Payments Industry Intelligence's explanation of why Berkshire sold out of Visa and Mastercard [[n0395]] is a reminder that Buffett sells as readily as he buys.
When the Narrative Breaks

The trade breaks if safe turns out to mean already priced. Buffett's own framing, buybacks on a merely mildly attractive path [[n0827]] alongside the lament about a lack of good investments, implies Berkshire sees its stock as fair rather than cheap, so Friday's 3.56% jump leaves less margin than believers assume. The observable line is the $307.67 close of twenty sessions earlier: a slide back there while the S&P 500 holds would say the letter bought no premium at all (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25). Concentration is the second trigger, because an Apple drawdown hits one of the Four Giants directly. And Monday opens on a weekend of SWIFT exclusions; a market that lurches lower will test whether retail holds Berkshire as a haven or sells it as a source of cash.

retail.title: Rheinmetall / RHM.DE — Germany becomes the war trade's buyer
parts: Why Retail Is Here

The war trade just found a sovereign customer. Germany committed €100 billion to defence spending [[n1228]], with Scholz framing the increase as a response to Putin's war [[n1229]] and POLITICO calling it a historic shift [[n1230]]. Rheinmetall had already closed Friday at €107.05, up 7.00% on the day, 11.00% over five sessions and 15.06% over twenty (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25), and US contractors moved with it, Lockheed Martin up 3.48% to $409.49 and Raytheon Technologies 4.11%. For the crowd that cheered war-friendly stocks on invasion day [[n0623]], this is confirmation: the trade now has a budget behind it.
Where It Breaks

A pledge is not a purchase order. The money still has to become contracts, procurement runs on years rather than weekends, and the risk for late buyers is paying for a decade of orders in a single gap. The BBC calls it a dramatic German U-turn [[n1232]]; the larger the turn, the longer the road from announcement to delivery. Watch the €93.04 close of twenty sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25): the further the shares run above it on promises alone, the more any delay in turning the pledge into orders would hurt.

retail.title: Block / SQ — the beaten fintech jumps by a quarter
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Block is the crowd's fintech, the payments name CNBC traces from a scrappy hardware start-up to a powerhouse [[n0584]], and after a brutal stretch for fintech it delivered the day believers wait for. Australian holders got there first, with ABC reporting Block soaring on the ASX [[n0061]]; then the US shares rose 26.14% to $119.82 on Friday, the first session after quarterly results in which, Payments Dive reports, the company defended higher marketing spending [[n1073]]. They are now up 15.19% over five sessions and 13.42% over twenty, and PayPal rose 5.64% the same day (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25). The emotional pull is the comeback: a name left for dead jumps by a quarter in a day, and every holder who stayed feels vindicated.
Where It Breaks

The bear case sits inside the same results: that marketing push [[n1073]] means part of the growth is being bought. The sector has not been forgiven, only Block's quarter, with PayPal still down 29.83% and Affirm 23.17% over twenty sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25). A slide back toward the $105.64 close of twenty sessions earlier would make Friday look like a relief burst rather than a new trend, and with the 2Y yield up 37 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2022-02-25), rates are no friend to a re-rating.

retail.title: MP Materials / MP — rare earths become a security trade
parts: Why Retail Is Here

The war has turned supply chains into a national-security story, and a US rare-earth miner is its simplest ticker. MP Materials reported higher profit as rare-earth prices surged [[n0595]], days after announcing a Department of Defense heavy rare-earth processing contract [[n0341]]. The stock rose 6.84% to $46.85 on Friday, 12.62% over five sessions and 25.10% over twenty, and Australia's Lynas Rare Earths gained 6.93% to A$9.57 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25). The crowd's pitch is simple: if the West cannot rely on hostile suppliers, the domestic miner becomes strategic, and strategic assets get bid.
Where It Breaks

The bid is a bet on prices staying high and governments staying generous. A 25.10% run in twenty sessions prices in a lot of both, and a commodity producer's earnings swing with the very rare-earth prices that just made the quarter. The Statesman's warning that the war could worsen the global chip shortage [[n1965]] cuts both ways, because the end markets for magnets need chips too. Watch the $37.45 close of twenty sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-25): a fade back toward it would say the security premium was a headline trade, not a re-rating.
